title: The Book of Creation
hook: an ancient short book on creation through letters and numbers

segments.voice: Yesterday, four sages walked into the orchard, and only one walked out in peace. Your line was enter carefully. Did you pause at a doorway, and ask who could walk you in? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

On the Torah's first page, the world gets made without hands. Not with tools. God speaks. "And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light." Over and over on that page: God said, and it was so. Sentences. Words. And words are made of letters. So a question follows, if you sit with that page long enough. What are the letters doing? Are they just how we write the story down, or are they part of how the story happened? A small, strange book takes that question all the way. Today's word is its name.
screen: `GOD SAID, AND IT WAS SO.` → `WORDS ARE MADE OF LETTERS.` → `WHAT ARE THE LETTERS DOING?`

segments.voice: Sefer Yetzirah. The Book of Creation, or the Book of Formation. It is short, and it reads less like a story and more like a riddle. Turn it four ways. First, its opening. The book says the world was created through paths of wisdom, and it names what those paths are made of: ten sefirot, and the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Ten and twenty-two, the book itself counts them. We'll meet that word, sefirot, again in a few days, grown much larger. Second, what it does with the letters. The book describes them being engraved, carved, weighed, combined and turned around, one with another, and says that with them everything that is formed was formed. Letters as building blocks, not just labels. Third, its company. The Talmud has its own small story in this direction: it says Bezalel, who built the tabernacle in the desert, knew how to join the letters by which heaven and earth were created. A craftsman whose real skill was the alphabet. Fourth, the name tradition puts on it. Some versions of the book end with Abraham, and tradition ties the book to him. Scholars ask other questions about its origins, and the book itself doesn't settle them. What it gives you instead is a way of looking. If the world was spoken, then every letter on the page has a little of the beginning in it. Kabbalists would build a great deal on this short book.
screen: `PATHS OF WISDOM.` · `LETTERS ENGRAVED, WEIGHED, COMBINED.` · `BEZALEL KNEW THE LETTERS.` · `A BOOK TIED TO ABRAHAM.` · then, large: `LETTERS CREATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the Hebrew letters. If you have a prayer book, a Torah, or even a picture of the alphabet on your phone, open it. If you don't read Hebrew, that's fine. You're not reading. You're looking. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes rest on one letter. Notice its shape: the open side, the closed side, the little crown or hook at its top. Stay with that one letter for a few breaths. Then move to the next one, slowly. Let each letter be a shape before it's a sound, and a sound before it's a word. The bell holds the time.
Sefer Yetzirah. The Book of Creation: a short, riddle-like book that describes the world formed through paths of wisdom, the sefirot and the Hebrew letters. Today's word.
Your line: letters create. Today, before you send a message, read one sentence of it back slowly, as if its letters were building something. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Sefer Yetzirah is studied as a foundational text of Kabbalah, usually alongside its commentaries, and some teachers begin by having students learn to look closely at the Hebrew letters themselves.

original.note: Hebrew: the book of formation, or of creation.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old book of numerology.
what it means: a short book that sees the Hebrew letters as part of how a spoken world was made.
what a scholar hears: Sefer Yetzirah's opening on the paths of wisdom, ten sefirot and twenty-two letters, and the Talmud's line that Bezalel knew how to join the letters of creation (Berakhot 55a).
